Will Worship
wil WUR-ship
noun phrase (Colossians 2:23)
From the Authorized Version rendering of the Greek ethelothreskeia (Colossians 2:23), “self-imposed worship”; worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God.

Biblical Definition

Will worship is worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God—the Authorized Version's rendering of the Greek ethelothreskeia, “self-chosen religion.” The apostle warns the Colossians against the ordinances and traditions of men, which “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.” Such worship looks pious—ascetic, humble, severe—but it is self-invented, resting on the commandments and doctrines of men, and the Lord pronounces it vain: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” The dictionary marks will worship as the precise opposite of the regulative principle of worship, which holds that God is to be worshipped only in the ways He has appointed in His Word. Whatsoever God commands in worship is required; whatsoever He has not commanded is forbidden, for He charged Israel, “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.” Will worship is the sin of adding—the will of man legislating for God how He shall be served. The dictionary marks it against the whole tide of self-styled worship: the inventions of Rome (images, relics, the multiplied rites and feasts), the asceticism that supposes self-denial earns merit, and equally the modern self-expressive worship that makes the worshipper's preference and feeling the rule, asking not “what has God commanded?” but “what do we like?” Both the old severity and the new spontaneity are will worship if they rest on the will of man rather than the Word of God. True worship is humble obedience: God to be served as He has prescribed, neither more nor less.

Webster 1828 Definition

Worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God (Colossians 2:23, Greek ethelothreskeia); the opposite of the regulative principle, condemned as vain (Matthew 15:9) whether in ascetic invention or modern self-expression.

WILL WORSHIP, noun phrase. [Greek ethelothreskeia, self-chosen religion.] Worship devised by man's will, not God's command.

It has “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility… not in any honour” (Colossians 2:23).

The Lord calls it vain: teaching for doctrines the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9).

The opposite of the regulative principle: God adds nor diminishes (Deuteronomy 12:32).

Found alike in ascetic invention and in modern self-expressive worship.

Key Scripture

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

Mt 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

De 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

Modern Corruption

Will worship is itself the corruption: man's will legislating for God how He shall be served—found in Rome's ascetic inventions and equally in modern self-expressive worship that asks “what do we like?” not “what has God commanded?”

expand to see more

Will worship is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. It is worship invented by the will of man and not commanded by God, and the apostle exposes it: it has a show of wisdom—ascetic, humble, severe—but rests on the commandments and doctrines of men, and the Lord calls such worship vain. The dictionary sets against it the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only as He has appointed, for He forbids adding to or diminishing from what He commands. To devise worship He has not authorized, however pious it appears, is to put the will of man in the place of the Word of God.

The dictionary marks two faces of the same sin. The old face is the ascetic and ceremonial invention—Rome's images, relics, multiplied rites and feasts, and the self-denial that supposes it earns merit. The new face, equally will worship, is the modern self-expressive worship that makes the worshipper's preference and feeling the rule, asking not “what has God commanded?” but “what moves us?” The dictionary names both: whether the will of man invents severity or invents spontaneity, it is still the will of man legislating for God. True worship is humble obedience—God served in the ways He has prescribed, neither more nor less, that the honour be His and not the worshipper's.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek ethelothreskeia (Colossians 2:23), from thelo (to will) and threskeia (religion, worship); “self-willed worship,” rendered “will worship” in the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

Ethelothreskeia, Greek, “self-chosen worship” (Colossians 2:23).

Thelo, Greek, to will or wish; threskeia, religion or worship.

The opposite of the regulative principle of worship.

Condemned as vain: “the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:9).

Forbidden by the rule against adding to God's commands (Deuteronomy 12:32).

Usage

"The pastor named the unbiblical rite will worship, a show of wisdom resting on the will of man."

"He applied the regulative principle: God adds nor diminishes, and will worship is the sin of adding."

"She saw that both ascetic invention and self-expressive worship are will worship if they rest on man's will."
